title: Class relationships, coupling and cohesion
scopeHtml: Scope: dependency, association, aggregation, composition, inheritance and realization, plus coupling and cohesion with class diagrams.

notes.title: Why relationships matter
notes.html:
Classes never live alone; the arrows between them decide how hard your code is to change. Choosing the right relationship answers: who creates whom, who owns whom, what dies together, and what breaks when something changes.

From weakest to strongest coupling: dependency, association, aggregation, composition, realization/inheritance (the last two are about type, not lifetime, but inheritance is the tightest).

  UML arrows (memorise these)
  A ..........> B     dependency   (dashed, open arrowhead)  A uses B briefly
  A ----------> B     association  (solid, open arrowhead)   A holds a reference to B
  A <>--------> B     aggregation  (hollow diamond on whole) A has B, B can live alone
  A <#>-------> B     composition  (filled diamond on whole) A owns B, B dies with A
  A ----------|> B    inheritance  (solid, hollow triangle)  A is-a B
  A ..........|> B    realization  (dashed, hollow triangle) A implements interface B

Worked example. In a food-delivery codebase of 400 classes, a Restaurant class with 30 outgoing arrows is a red flag: any change in 30 places can break it. The target is a graph where most arrows point at stable interfaces.

Industry examples. Martin Fowler's and the UML spec's notation is the interview standard. Tools such as IntelliJ's "Diagrams" and Structure101 report coupling per package so teams catch cycles.

Everyday analogy. Friendships: borrowing a pen (dependency), having a contact in your phone (association), a team and its players (aggregation), your body and your heart (composition).

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing every arrow as a plain line; interviewers want to see the diamond and the arrowhead.
  • Mixing up which end the diamond goes on: it sits on the owner/whole.

notes.title: Dependency: uses briefly
notes.html:
A depends on B when A only needs B for a moment, as a parameter, local variable or return value, not as stored state. Change B's method signature and A may break.

class InvoiceService {
    // Dependency: Clock and PdfWriter appear only inside the method
    byte[] render(Invoice inv, PdfWriter writer, Clock clock) {
        return writer.write(inv, clock.instant());
    }
}
class InvoiceService {
    fun render(inv: Invoice, writer: PdfWriter, clock: Clock): ByteArray = writer.write(inv, clock.instant())
}

Before (hidden dependency, hard to test):

class InvoiceService {
    byte[] render(Invoice inv) {
        Instant now = Instant.now();                 // hidden global dependency on the system clock
        return new PdfWriter().write(inv, now);      // hidden dependency created inside
    }
}

After: pass them in (above). A test now fixes the clock at 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z and asserts the exact bytes.

Worked example. 40 tests that read Instant.now() become flaky around midnight and month end. Injecting Clock makes all 40 deterministic, and runtime drops since no sleep is needed.

Industry examples. Dagger/Hilt (Android), Spring and Guice exist mainly to make dependencies visible and swappable. java.time.Clock was added in Java 8 for exactly this reason.

Everyday analogy. Borrowing a stapler for one task and giving it back.

Decision gravity. Dependencies are the cheapest and most reversible relationship. Hidden dependencies (static calls, new inside methods) are the expensive ones because tests cannot replace them.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling any method call a dependency; the useful distinction is "stored in a field or not".
  • Static singletons (Config.get()) are dependencies with no arrow in the signature.

notes.title: Association: knows about
notes.html:
Association means A holds a reference to B as a field and can call it over time, but neither owns the other. It may be one-way or two-way, with multiplicity (1, 0..1, 1..*, *).

class Order {
    private final Customer customer;       // many orders -> one customer (* to 1)
    Order(Customer c) { this.customer = c; }
}
class Customer { /* does NOT hold orders: one-way association */ }
class Order(private val customer: Customer)
  Order  *  -------------->  1  Customer
         (orders)               (customer)

Worked example. A bidirectional link (Customer.orders and Order.customer) means both sides must be kept in sync. Adding an order requires two updates; forgetting one gives inconsistent in-memory state. With a one-way link, you query orders by customerId when needed: 1 index on orders(customer_id) and one source of truth.

Industry examples. JPA/Hibernate @ManyToOne / @OneToMany(mappedBy=...) is association; the mappedBy side is the inverse, and Hibernate famously produces N+1 queries (1 query for 100 customers plus 100 for their orders) if you walk the association lazily in a loop. Fix with JOIN FETCH or batch fetching.

Everyday analogy. A phone contact: you can call them, but your contact list does not own them.

Decision gravity. Prefer one-way associations (cheap, simple). Making them two-way later is easy; removing a two-way association after many callers use both ends is a one-way door.

Common interview traps.

  • Bidirectional JSON serialisation causing infinite recursion (StackOverflowError).
  • Holding a reference to a whole object when only its id is needed (couples aggregates; in DDD reference other aggregates by id).

notes.title: Aggregation: has, but does not own
notes.html:
Aggregation is a "whole-part" association where the part can exist without the whole. A Team has Players, but if the team is disbanded the players still exist.

class Team {
    private final List<Player> players = new ArrayList<>();
    void add(Player p) { players.add(p); }        // player created elsewhere, passed in
}
class Team { private val players = mutableListOf<Player>(); fun add(p: Player) { players += p } }
  Team <>---------- 0..* Player      (hollow diamond at Team)

Worked example. A Playlist aggregates Songs: delete a playlist of 50 songs and the 50 songs remain in the library. In the database that is a join table playlist_song(playlist_id, song_id) with no ON DELETE CASCADE to song.

Industry examples. Spotify playlists and songs, a Kubernetes Service and its Pods (the Service selects pods, does not own them), a Slack channel and its members.

Everyday analogy. A book club and its members: the club ends, the people stay.

Decision gravity. Aggregation is a modelling choice, not a language feature: Java has no keyword. It is reversible. The cost of the wrong choice shows up at delete time: orphan data or accidental data loss.

Common interview traps.

  • Many candidates say UML aggregation is "weak composition" with no behavioural difference; in code the difference is who creates and who controls lifetime. Say that.
  • Even the UML spec authors admitted aggregation is vague; be ready to explain via lifetime.

notes.title: Composition: owns and controls life
notes.html:
Composition is a strong whole-part link where the part cannot exist without the whole and dies with it. The whole creates the part and no one else holds a reference to it.

class Order {
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();    // created and owned here
    void addLine(String sku, int qty) { lines.add(new OrderLine(sku, qty)); }
    List<OrderLine> lines() { return List.copyOf(lines); }      // never leak the owned parts
}
class OrderLine { /* package-private constructor: only Order creates it */ }
class Order {
    private val _lines = mutableListOf<OrderLine>()
    val lines: List<OrderLine> get() = _lines.toList()
    fun addLine(sku: String, qty: Int) { _lines += OrderLine(sku, qty) }
}
  Order <#>---------- 1..* OrderLine    (filled diamond at Order)
  Delete Order -> OrderLines are deleted too
CREATE TABLE order_line (
  order_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  line_no  INT NOT NULL,
  sku      TEXT NOT NULL,
  qty      INT NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no)
);

Worked example. Order with 3 lines; delete the order, 3 lines vanish through ON DELETE CASCADE. With aggregation by mistake, you would leave 3 orphan rows per deleted order; at 10,000 deletions a day that is 30,000 junk rows a day, a month later 900,000 rows in a table nobody can explain.

Industry examples. Domain-Driven Design calls this an aggregate: Order is the root and the only door to its lines, so invariants like "total = sum of lines" live in one place. A Postgres table and its indexes, or Android Activity and its Views, show the same ownership.

Everyday analogy. A house and its rooms: demolish the house and the rooms are gone.

Decision gravity. Composition is the most useful relationship for protecting invariants and is easy to start with. Leaking the part (returning the internal list or giving a reference to another object) quietly turns composition into association, a silent one-way door.

Common interview traps.

  • Using composition language but passing the part in from outside (that is aggregation).
  • The phrase "composition over inheritance" uses the word loosely for any has-a; know the UML meaning too.
  • Cascading deletes on huge parents can lock millions of rows; batch them.

notes.title: Inheritance and realization
notes.html:
Inheritance (generalisation) means is-a between classes; realization means a class implements an interface. Both are type relationships, and both bind the child to the parent's contract.

interface Payment { void pay(long cents); }                  // realization target
abstract class BasePayment implements Payment {              // inheritance + realization
    protected void log(String m) { System.out.println(m); }
}
class UpiPayment extends BasePayment { public void pay(long c) { log("UPI " + c); } }
interface Payment { fun pay(cents: Long) }
abstract class BasePayment : Payment { protected fun log(m: String) = println(m) }
class UpiPayment : BasePayment() { override fun pay(cents: Long) = log("UPI $cents") }
      <<interface>> Payment
            ^  (dashed, hollow triangle)  = realization
            |
       BasePayment {abstract}
            ^  (solid, hollow triangle)   = inheritance
            |
        UpiPayment

Worked example. A 3-level hierarchy with 5 subclasses where each overrides 2 of 8 methods gives 10 override sites to reason about. A change in the base touches all 5. Realising one interface plus delegating shared code to a helper keeps each class self-contained.

Industry examples. Java collections: List (interface) realised by ArrayList; AbstractList gives shared code. Android: Context / ContextWrapper (decorator-style delegation rather than deep inheritance).

Everyday analogy. An interface is a job description; a base class is a relative's family business that you join and inherit habits from.

Decision gravity. Realization is cheap and highly reversible. Class inheritance is the strongest coupling in the language (see the pillars note). Prefer realizing interfaces and delegating to collaborators.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing realization (implements) and inheritance (extends) arrows: dashed vs solid.
  • Deep hierarchies (more than 2 to 3 levels) that nobody can navigate.

notes.title: Coupling: how tightly linked
notes.html:
Coupling is how much one module must know about another to work. Low coupling means a change in B rarely forces a change in A. Aim for loose coupling.

Levels from worst to best:

  1. Content coupling: A reaches into B's internals (public fields, reflection).
  2. Common coupling: both share global mutable state.
  3. Control coupling: A passes a flag that tells B what to do.
  4. Stamp/data coupling: A passes a large object when B needs two fields.
  5. Message coupling: A calls B through a small stable interface.

Before (control + stamp coupling):

void export(Order o, String format) {                   // flag controls behaviour
    if (format.equals("CSV")) writeCsv(o);              // needs only o.id() and o.total()
    else writeJson(o);
}

After (message coupling through an interface):

interface Exporter { void export(long orderId, long totalCents); }
class CsvExporter implements Exporter { public void export(long id, long t) { /* ... */ } }
fun interface Exporter { fun export(orderId: Long, totalCents: Long) }

Worked example. Module A calls 3 methods of B: coupling is low. Module A reads 14 fields of B and subclasses it: a change in B breaks 17 places. Measure with fan-out (outgoing dependencies) and fan-in; keep fan-out under about 7 to 10 per class as a rule of thumb. Also track temporal coupling (must call init() before run()) and deployment coupling (two microservices that must be released together are a distributed monolith).

Industry examples. Amazon's rule that teams talk only through APIs (the "API mandate") is decoupling at organisation scale. Netflix breaks coupling with events and circuit breakers so one failing service does not take down another.

Everyday analogy. Two trains linked by a thin coupling you can unhook versus two rooms welded together.

Decision gravity. Coupling you introduce quietly in week 1 becomes the rewrite in year 3. Seams (interfaces, events) are cheap early and expensive late. But decoupling everything costs indirection; decouple where change is likely.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "zero coupling" is the goal; modules must interact, so aim for the lowest necessary and explicit coupling.
  • Counting only class-level coupling and ignoring shared databases between services.

notes.title: Cohesion: how focused
notes.html:
Cohesion is how strongly the parts of one class belong together. High cohesion means a class does one job and its methods use the same fields. Aim for high cohesion with low coupling.

Warning sign: a UserManager with login(), sendEmail(), generateReport(), resizeAvatar(); methods share nothing. A quick test is LCOM (lack of cohesion of methods): if you can split the fields into groups and each method touches only one group, split the class.

Before (low cohesion):

class UserManager {
    private DbPool db; private SmtpClient smtp; private ImageLib img;
    void login(String u, String p) { /* uses db */ }
    void sendWelcome(String u)     { /* uses smtp */ }
    byte[] resizeAvatar(byte[] b)  { /* uses img */ }
}

After (three focused classes):

class AuthService   { private final DbPool db;      void login(String u, String p) { } }
class MailService   { private final SmtpClient smtp; void sendWelcome(String u) { } }
class AvatarService { private final ImageLib img;   byte[] resize(byte[] b) { } }
class AuthService(private val db: DbPool) { fun login(u: String, p: String) {} }
class MailService(private val smtp: SmtpClient) { fun sendWelcome(u: String) {} }
class AvatarService(private val img: ImageLib) { fun resize(b: ByteArray): ByteArray = b }
 Before: UserManager --> {DbPool, SmtpClient, ImageLib}    (3 unrelated reasons to change)
 After:  AuthService --> DbPool
         MailService --> SmtpClient
         AvatarService --> ImageLib

Worked example. UserManager of 1,800 lines is touched by 5 teams in a quarter, giving about 25 merge conflicts and a test class needing 3 mocks per test. After splitting, each class is 300 to 600 lines, has 1 mock per test, and conflicts drop sharply. Git churn (files with the most commits) combined with size is a good smell detector.

Industry examples. Google's and Spotify's squad/service ownership follows high cohesion at team level. Unix tools (grep, sort) are the classic highly cohesive units that compose through pipes.

Everyday analogy. A toolbox where each drawer holds one kind of tool versus a junk drawer.

Decision gravity. Splitting a class is reversible and low risk with good tests. Splitting too much (a class per method) increases coupling and navigation cost; balance with the Single Responsibility Principle: one reason to change, not one method.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up the two: cohesion is inside a module, coupling is between modules.
  • "God class" is the standard name for the low-cohesion extreme; know a fix (extract class, move method).
  • Layered anti-patterns: a Utils class is low cohesion by design.

notes.title: Choosing the right relationship
notes.html:
Use this decision path when drawing a class diagram in an interview.

Question Answer Draw
Only a parameter or local? yes dependency (dashed arrow)
Field, independent lifetime? yes association (line), or aggregation if whole-part
Created and destroyed by owner? yes composition (filled diamond)
Is-a, fully substitutable? yes inheritance (solid, hollow triangle)
Implements a contract? yes realization (dashed, hollow triangle)

Worked example: parking lot. ParkingLot <#> Floor <#> Slot (composition: slots die with the floor). Ticket associates with Vehicle and Slot (association, ticket does not own them). ParkingLot uses FeeCalculator (interface; realization by HourlyFee). Gate depends on Ticket only as a parameter (dependency). Stating each arrow's reason aloud earns credit.

Industry examples. DDD aggregates (Eric Evans) formalise composition boundaries; the Spring ApplicationContext owns its beans (composition) while beans reference each other by association.

Everyday analogy. A school: classrooms (composition), students enrolled (aggregation), a guest speaker for one session (dependency).

Decision gravity. The choice between aggregation and composition is a lifetime and delete-cascade decision you will live with in your schema; changing it later means a data migration, which makes it nearly a one-way door once production data exists.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing everything as composition because it "looks strong"; that implies cascading deletes.
  • Leaving out multiplicities (1, 0..1, 1..*).
  • Putting implementation detail (private helpers) in a high-level class diagram.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Relationships from loosest to tightest: dependency, association, aggregation, composition, then inheritance/realization.
  • Dependency = used inside a method; make hidden ones visible by injecting them.
  • Association = a field reference; prefer one-way, avoid needless bidirectional links.
  • Aggregation = part outlives whole; composition = part dies with whole, owner creates it and never leaks it (DDD aggregate root).
  • Inheritance is a type relationship and the strongest coupling; realization of interfaces is cheap and reversible.
  • Coupling is between modules (aim low, explicit, via small interfaces); cohesion is inside a module (aim high, one reason to change).
  • In an interview, justify every arrow with lifetime, ownership and multiplicity.

questions.promptHtml: Explain dependency, association, aggregation and composition with one example each, and how you decide which arrow to draw.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the base of every class diagram round; a weak answer shows you cannot reason about ownership and lifetime.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Dependency: A uses B only inside a method. Association: A keeps B in a field. Aggregation: A has B but B can outlive A. Composition: A owns B, creates it and B dies with A. I decide by asking: parameter or local? field? who creates it? can it outlive the owner?

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From loosest to tightest coupling: dependency, association, aggregation, composition, then inheritance/realization (type relationships).

A ..........> B   dependency (dashed arrow)
A ----------> B   association (solid arrow)
A <>--------> B   aggregation (hollow diamond on the whole)
A <#>-------> B   composition (filled diamond on the whole)

Examples: InvoiceService.render(Invoice, PdfWriter) depends on PdfWriter; Order associates with Customer; Team aggregates Player; Order is composed of OrderLine. The diamond sits on the owner. Add multiplicities (1, 0..1, 1..*).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Order {
    private final Customer customer;                         // association
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>(); // composition (created here)
    Order(Customer c) { this.customer = c; }
    void addLine(String sku, int q) { lines.add(new OrderLine(sku, q)); }
    byte[] render(PdfWriter w) { return w.write(this); }      // dependency
}
class Order(private val customer: Customer) {
    private val lines = mutableListOf<OrderLine>()
    fun addLine(sku: String, q: Int) { lines += OrderLine(sku, q) }
    fun render(w: PdfWriter): ByteArray = w.write(this)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Drawing every arrow as a plain line.
  • Putting the diamond on the wrong end.
  • Calling every field composition.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Java have a keyword for aggregation? -> No; it is a modelling choice about lifetime and who creates the part.
  2. Which relationship is cheapest to change? -> Dependency; inheritance is the tightest.
  3. How does it show in the database? -> Composition: child FK with ON DELETE CASCADE; aggregation: join table without cascade to the part.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives the definitions. Senior justifies each arrow with ownership, lifetime and delete behaviour, and mentions multiplicity.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Wrong lifetime choices appear as orphan rows or accidental deletes in the schema.

questions.promptHtml: What is the real difference between aggregation and composition in code, not just in the diagram?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates repeat "weak vs strong"; the interviewer wants to hear lifetime and who controls creation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In composition the whole creates the part and controls its lifetime, nobody else holds a reference, and deleting the whole deletes the parts. In aggregation the part is created elsewhere and passed in, and it survives the whole. The tell in code is new OrderLine(...) inside the owner versus a part handed in through a method or constructor.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Composition protects invariants: Order is the only door to its lines, so "total equals sum of lines" lives in one place (DDD aggregate root). It stays composition only if you never leak the part: returning the internal list or handing a line to another object quietly turns it into association. In SQL, composition is a child table with ON DELETE CASCADE; aggregation is a join table without cascade to the part.

Order <#>---- 1..* OrderLine     delete Order -> lines deleted
Playlist <>---- 0..* Song        delete Playlist -> songs remain

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CREATE TABLE order_line (
  order_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  line_no  INT NOT NULL,
  sku TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no)
);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Composition language but part passed in from outside.
  • Drawing everything as composition, implying cascading deletes.
  • Cascading delete of millions of child rows in one transaction (lock and log pressure; batch it).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does composition turn into association by accident? -> A getter returns the internal list or part.
  2. Spotify playlist and song? -> Aggregation; songs persist when a playlist is deleted.
  3. What is a DDD aggregate? -> A cluster treated as one unit with a root; outside code references the root only.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "strong vs weak". Senior says lifetime, creation and leak-protection, and ties it to schema cascade.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Mislabeling a link as aggregation left 30,000 orphan rows a day in one team's table.

questions.promptHtml: What are coupling and cohesion, and how would you measure or spot problems in a codebase?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They are the two quality axes behind most design advice; an applied answer shows experience with real refactors.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Coupling is how much one module must know about another; I want it low and explicit, through small interfaces. Cohesion is how well the parts of one class belong together; I want it high, one reason to change. I spot problems with fan-out, churn and size, a class touched by many teams, or one needing many mocks per test.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Coupling levels from worst to best: content (reaching into internals), common (shared global state), control (passing a flag that steers behaviour), stamp/data (passing a big object when two fields suffice), message (small stable interface). Also watch temporal coupling (init() before run()) and deployment coupling (services that must release together are a distributed monolith).

Cohesion test: if fields split into groups and each method touches only one group, split the class (LCOM). Smell metrics: fan-out above roughly 7 to 10, files with high git churn and size, 3+ mocks per test.

Low cohesion:  UserManager --> {DbPool, SmtpClient, ImageLib}
Fix:           AuthService --> DbPool ; MailService --> SmtpClient ; AvatarService --> ImageLib

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void export(Order o, String format) { if (format.equals("CSV")) writeCsv(o); else writeJson(o); } // control + stamp coupling
interface Exporter { void export(long orderId, long totalCents); }                                 // message coupling
fun interface Exporter { fun export(orderId: Long, totalCents: Long) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying zero coupling is the goal.
  • Mixing them up: cohesion is inside a module, coupling between modules.
  • Ignoring shared databases between services.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Fan-in vs fan-out? -> Incoming vs outgoing dependencies; high fan-in classes must be stable, high fan-out ones are fragile.
  2. Is Utils a problem? -> It is low cohesion by design.
  3. Two microservices share a DB table. Coupling? -> Content/common coupling at architecture level; schema change forces both to deploy together.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "low coupling, high cohesion". Senior ranks coupling kinds, gives measurable smells and warns against over-decoupling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 1,800-line UserManager touched by 5 teams produced about 25 merge conflicts a quarter.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between inheritance and realization, and why do experienced developers lean on realization?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests UML arrow knowledge and whether you understand why implements is safer than extends.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Inheritance (extends, solid line with hollow triangle) is is-a between classes and shares state and code. Realization (implements, dashed line with hollow triangle) means the class fulfils an interface contract. Realization binds you only to a contract, so it is cheap and reversible; class inheritance is the tightest coupling Java offers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A child object holds the parent's fields, can be upcast, and runs the parent constructor first. Parent changes can silently break children. With an interface, shared code goes into a helper collaborator you delegate to, so each class stays self-contained.

   <<interface>> Payment
         ^   (dashed)  realization
   BasePayment {abstract}
         ^   (solid)   inheritance
     UpiPayment

Depth guideline: more than 2 to 3 levels is hard to navigate. 5 subclasses overriding 2 of 8 methods each gives 10 override sites to reason about.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Payment { void pay(long cents); }
abstract class BasePayment implements Payment { protected void log(String m) { System.out.println(m); } }
class UpiPayment extends BasePayment { public void pay(long c) { log("UPI " + c); } }
interface Payment { fun pay(cents: Long) }
abstract class BasePayment : Payment { protected fun log(m: String) = println(m) }
class UpiPayment : BasePayment() { override fun pay(cents: Long) = log("UPI $cents") }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Swapping dashed and solid arrows.
  • Deep hierarchies nobody can navigate.
  • Inheriting just for code reuse when has-a fits.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Java collections example? -> List interface realised by ArrayList; AbstractList is a skeleton base class.
  2. How do you reuse code without inheriting? -> Delegate to a collaborator; Kotlin by.
  3. When is inheritance justified? -> Stable true is-a, substitutable, designed for it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "extends vs implements". Senior ties it to coupling, one-way-door cost and delegation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A base-class change in a shared module broke 5 subclasses across teams in one release.

questions.contextHtml:
CI has 40 tests that sporadically fail, always between 23:55 and 00:05 UTC and on month-end. All involve InvoiceService, which does Instant.now() and new PdfWriter() inside render. Failure sample:

expected: <2026-01-31 invoice due 2026-03-02>
 but was: <2026-02-01 invoice due 2026-03-03>
FAILED: InvoiceServiceTest.dueDateIsThirtyDaysOut  (0.9 s)

A red herring: the team suspects the test DB.
questions.promptHtml: Why flaky, and how do you fix both the tests and the design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries to CI" or Thread.sleep to cross midnight. It hides the nondeterminism.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do the failures correlate with wall-clock time? Is the clock used anywhere else? Do we use a DI framework?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Quarantine the flaky tests so they stop blocking merges, with a ticket.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Hidden dependency on the system clock; test data crossing a date boundary; time zone mismatch; DB (unlikely).
  4. How I'd verify: Re-run with the system clock faked via a faketime run; grep for Instant.now(, LocalDate.now(.
  5. Root cause: Instant.now() and new PdfWriter() are dependencies with no arrow in the signature; tests cannot control them.
  6. Fix: Inject them.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class InvoiceService {
    private final Clock clock; private final PdfWriter writer;
    InvoiceService(Clock c, PdfWriter w) { clock = c; writer = w; }
    byte[] render(Invoice inv) { return writer.write(inv, clock.instant()); }
}
// test: Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-01-31T23:59:59Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC)
class InvoiceService(private val clock: Clock, private val writer: PdfWriter) {
    fun render(inv: Invoice): ByteArray = writer.write(inv, clock.instant())
}
  1. Prevention: Ban Instant.now() outside the composition root (ArchUnit rule); run date-edge cases (month end, leap day, DST) as parameterised tests.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Static mocking tools (mockStatic) work but are a workaround for a design smell. I would not add sleeps.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does the clock inject into every class? -> Only into classes that need time; one Clock bean.
  • Production runs in UTC but tests in IST? -> Use Clock with explicit zone.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A billing test suite went green permanently after clock injection and its runtime dropped by minutes since sleeps disappeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries.
  • Hire: injects Clock.
  • Strong hire: also fixes new inside, adds ArchUnit guard and edge-date tests.

questions.contextHtml:
After adding Customer.orders to an existing Order.customer link, two problems appear. The API for GET /customers/7 returns HTTP 500 with a stack trace, and the customer list page, 100 customers, becomes slow.

java.lang.StackOverflowError
  at com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ser.BeanPropertySerializer.serializeAsField
  at ... Customer["orders"]->Order["customer"]->Customer["orders"]...
SQL log: 1 query for customers + 100 queries "select * from orders where customer_id=?" (210 ms total)
questions.promptHtml: Explain both symptoms, and decide whether the bidirectional link stays.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: @JsonIgnore and move on. That fixes the 500 but not the model or the N+1.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who needs customer.orders in memory? Do the pages need orders or just counts? Is this JPA/Hibernate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Return DTOs, not entities, so the API stops recursing; hotfix list page with JOIN FETCH or a batch size.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cyclic serialisation of entities; lazy collection triggered per customer (N+1); out-of-sync sides.
  4. How I'd verify: SQL logs counting statements; a test asserting statement count.
  5. Root cause: Two-way association exposes a cycle to serialisation and a lazy walk in a loop.
  6. Fix: Prefer one-way: keep Order.customer, remove Customer.orders, query by customerId.
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?;      -- or WHERE customer_id IN (...) for 100 customers
  1. Prevention: DTO boundary; query-count assertions in tests; keep associations one-way unless both directions are needed.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Removing the back-reference later after many callers use it is a one-way door; adding it later is cheap. I would not keep FetchType.EAGER everywhere; it hides N+1 and loads too much.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need orders per customer page? -> One query with the IN list, then group in memory.
  • Keeping both sides in sync? -> Update both in one method, or avoid.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "harmless" back-reference turned a 40 ms list endpoint into 2 s once a customer had 800 orders.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: @JsonIgnore only.
  • Hire: DTOs and join fetch.
  • Strong hire: argues for the one-way model and statement-count tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A nightly job deletes 10,000 cancelled orders. DBA reports order_line has grown from 2M to 2.9M rows in 30 days although order count is flat, and storage alerts fire. The schema:

CREATE TABLE order_line (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id BIGINT NOT NULL,   -- no foreign key
  sku TEXT, qty INT
);
-- orphan check
SELECT count(*) FROM order_line ol LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = ol.order_id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
-- 900000
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong in the model, and how do you clean up and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run a cleanup script." It ignores that the model allowed orphans, and a one-shot DELETE of 900k rows locks the table.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can lines exist without an order in any business case? Do other tables reference order_line? Is there a retention/audit requirement?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop adding to the problem: change the delete job to delete lines first within one transaction.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Lines modelled as aggregation (no FK, no cascade) when they are composition; delete code path forgot lines; other jobs delete orders.
  4. How I'd verify: The orphan query above; look for all DELETE FROM orders call sites.
  5. Root cause: Lifetime was not encoded: lines die with the order, but nothing says so.
  6. Fix: Short term: delete orphans in batches. Long term: FK with cascade.
DELETE FROM order_line WHERE id IN (
  SELECT ol.id FROM order_line ol LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = ol.order_id
  WHERE o.id IS NULL LIMIT 10000);            -- repeat until 0 rows

ALTER TABLE order_line ADD CONSTRAINT fk_order
  FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE order_line VALIDATE CONSTRAINT fk_order;    -- after cleanup
  1. Prevention: Model parts as composition inside an aggregate; schema review checklist: every child table has an FK; orphan-count metric.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Cascade on huge parents can lock and generate lots of WAL, so I batch deletes for large parents. I would not cascade where children are shared (that is aggregation).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Soft deletes? -> Then cascade does not fire; mark children too or filter by parent state.
  • 900k rows already; can I add the FK directly? -> Not until orphans are removed; NOT VALID then VALIDATE.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reporting query joined orders to lines and silently double counted; the root cause was years of orphans from a deleted-order path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one-off script.
  • Hire: identifies composition and adds FK with cascade.
  • Strong hire: batches cleanup, uses NOT VALID, adds monitoring.

questions.contextHtml:
UserManager is 1,800 lines, changed by 5 teams, about 25 merge conflicts per quarter, and each unit test needs 3 mocks plus a 90-line setup. Fields and methods:

class UserManager {
    private DbPool db; private SmtpClient smtp; private ImageLib img;
    void login(String u, String p) { /* db */ }
    void sendWelcome(String u) { /* smtp */ }
    byte[] resizeAvatar(byte[] b) { /* img */ }
    String generateReport(String u) { /* db + formatting */ }
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and what is your refactor plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Split it into smaller files" or one class per method. Moves the lines but not the responsibilities.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which methods change together (git log)? Test coverage today? Any API consumers calling UserManager directly?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze new methods; add characterization tests around the public methods.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Low cohesion: field groups (db / smtp / img) used by disjoint method groups; "manager" naming invites dumping.
  4. How I'd verify: git log --format= --name-only | sort | uniq -c; LCOM per class; field-to-method usage matrix.
  5. Root cause: Four reasons to change in one class (auth, mail, images, reporting).
  6. Fix: Extract Class per cohesive group; move methods with the fields they use.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class AuthService   { private final DbPool db;      void login(String u, String p) { } }
class MailService   { private final SmtpClient smtp; void sendWelcome(String u) { } }
class AvatarService { private final ImageLib img;   byte[] resize(byte[] b) { } }
class UserReport    { private final DbPool db;      String generate(String u) { } }
class AuthService(private val db: DbPool) { fun login(u: String, p: String) {} }
class MailService(private val smtp: SmtpClient) { fun sendWelcome(u: String) {} }
class AvatarService(private val img: ImageLib) { fun resize(b: ByteArray): ByteArray = b }
  1. Prevention: Size/churn dashboard; review rule: a class with more than 3 collaborators from unrelated domains gets questioned; ban Manager/Utils names.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Splitting too far (a class per method) raises coupling and navigation cost. Keep a thin facade temporarily so callers migrate gradually.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Login also needs to send a welcome mail on first login? -> AuthService depends on a small WelcomeNotifier interface, not MailService internals.
  • How do you know when to stop? -> When each class has one reason to change and 1 to 2 mocks per test.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After splitting a 2,000-line class into four, merge conflicts fell sharply and tests dropped from 3 mocks to 1.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: split by file size.
  • Hire: Extract Class by field groups with tests.
  • Strong hire: uses churn data, keeps a facade and warns about over-splitting.

questions.contextHtml:
A music app deleted playlist "Old stuff" (50 songs). Next morning support gets tickets: 50 songs vanished from users' libraries and from other playlists. Code and schema:

@Entity class Playlist {
    @ManyToMany(cascade = CascadeType.REMOVE)     // songs owned by the playlist?
    @JoinTable(name = "playlist_song") List<Song> songs;
}
void deletePlaylist(long id) { playlistRepo.delete(playlistRepo.getReferenceById(id)); }
Hibernate SQL on delete:
delete from playlist_song where playlist_id=?
delete from song where id=?        -- x 50
questions.promptHtml: Why did songs disappear and what is the right model?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restore from backup and add a confirmation dialog." Treats a modelling bug as user error.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which cascade fired, ORM or DB? Do songs belong to the library independently? Can I restore from PITR safely without losing newer data?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the delete endpoint; restore the song rows from backup or PITR into a side table and merge.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: ORM CascadeType.REMOVE on the playlist-to-song mapping (the SQL log shows delete from song); a DB-level cascade (unlikely: a cascade on a link table only removes link rows).
  4. How I'd verify: Read the Hibernate SQL log; inspect the mapping; replay the delete on a restored copy.
  5. Root cause: Playlist-song is aggregation (a song outlives any playlist), but the mapping declared composition-style cascade, so deleting the playlist deleted its songs.
  6. Fix: Remove the cascade; deleting a playlist removes only link rows.
@ManyToMany                                        // no cascade REMOVE
@JoinTable(name = "playlist_song") List<Song> songs;
  1. Prevention: Schema/mapping review by lifetime question: "can B outlive A?"; a test that deleting a playlist leaves its songs.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use soft-delete as a substitute for modelling lifetime correctly, nor rely on a confirmation dialog.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Song deleted by admin, must disappear from playlists? -> Delete link rows explicitly in the same transaction.
  • Orphan links? -> FK ensures none.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "shared tag" table had cascade from the parent and wiped tags used by 3,000 other items.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restores and adds a dialog.
  • Hire: finds the wrong cascade and fixes it.
  • Strong hire: separates link-row cascade from part deletion, tests and recovery.

questions.contextHtml:
An Order has OrderLines and a stored total. A bug report says orders show total Rs 4,200 while lines sum to Rs 3,700. Audit finds one caller doing order.lines().get(0).setQty(1). Code:

class Order {
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    private long total;
    void addLine(OrderLine l) { lines.add(l); total += l.price() * l.qty(); }
    List<OrderLine> lines() { return lines; }
}
class OrderLine { long price; int qty; OrderLine(long p, int q) { price = p; qty = q; } }
questions.promptHtml: What relationship was intended, what did the code do instead, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Recompute total on read." Hides the symptom; any caller can still mutate lines and break other rules (stock, discounts).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can a line change after creation? Who creates OrderLine? Do other aggregates reference lines?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix affected totals with a one-off reconciliation query; wrap lines() in an unmodifiable view.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Leaked internal list; public mutable OrderLine; stored derived value.
  4. How I'd verify: Grep .lines() mutators; test that mutating the returned list throws.
  5. Root cause: Intended composition (Order owns lines and the total invariant), but leaking the parts turned it into association.
  6. Fix: Order creates lines; lines are immutable; total derived.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
final class Order {
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    void addLine(String sku, long price, int qty) { lines.add(new OrderLine(sku, price, qty)); }
    void changeQty(int idx, int qty) { lines.set(idx, lines.get(idx).withQty(qty)); }
    List<OrderLine> lines() { return List.copyOf(lines); }
    long total() { return lines.stream().mapToLong(l -> l.price() * l.qty()).sum(); }
}
record OrderLine(String sku, long price, int qty) { OrderLine withQty(int q) { return new OrderLine(sku, price, q); } }
class Order {
    private val _lines = mutableListOf<OrderLine>()
    val lines: List<OrderLine> get() = _lines.toList()
    fun addLine(sku: String, price: Long, qty: Int) { _lines += OrderLine(sku, price, qty) }
    fun total() = _lines.sumOf { it.price * it.qty }
}
data class OrderLine(val sku: String, val price: Long, val qty: Int)
  1. Prevention: Immutable value objects; a test asserting lines() is not mutable; a package-private constructor so only Order creates lines.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Computing total each time costs O(n), fine for tens of lines; cache with invalidation only if measured. I would not make OrderLine mutable with setters "for convenience".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 5,000 lines per order? -> Cache the total inside Order, updated only in addLine/changeQty.
  • Persistence layer needs setters? -> Use field access or a constructor mapping; keep the domain API closed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A discount engine mutated line prices through a leaked list and the invoice no longer matched the payment.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: recompute only.
  • Hire: copies list, derives total.
  • Strong hire: names composition leak, immutable parts, controls creation.

questions.contextHtml:
Two services, orders and inventory, share the stock table in one Postgres. A column rename in inventory last week broke orders in production for 22 minutes (error rate 9%). Both services must be released together to change anything in stock. Orders also calls inventory with a flag: reserve(sku, qty, mode="STRICT"). Leadership wants "microservices, so independent teams".

orders: ERROR column "qty_available" does not exist   (x 14,200 in 22 min)
inventory deploy v142 at 10:03; orders unchanged since v97
questions.promptHtml: Where is the coupling, what do you change first, and what do you not touch?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Split the database right away" or "add more integration tests". The first is risky under live traffic, the second does not remove the coupling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which service owns the stock data? What are orders' actual reads/writes? Can we tolerate eventual consistency for reads? Release cadence?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back v142 or add a view that restores the old column name; the incident shows content coupling through the shared schema.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Shared table (content/common coupling), plus control coupling via mode; deployment coupling (distributed monolith).
  4. How I'd verify: List queries touching stock per service from pg_stat_statements; dependency diagram; contract test results.
  5. Root cause: The database is the integration API, with no versioned contract.
  6. Fix: Short term: inventory exposes a view or versioned API (GET /stock/{sku}) and orders reads through it; add consumer-driven contract tests. Long term: inventory owns the table; orders keeps a local read model fed by events (verify the consistency needs first).
Before: orders --SQL--> stock <--SQL-- inventory    (schema = API)
After:  orders --HTTP v1/events--> inventory --SQL--> stock
  1. Prevention: Rule: one service writes a table, others use its API; expand-contract migrations; contract tests in CI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A network call adds latency and a failure mode (timeouts, retries); not every shared read needs a service. I would not split the database in one step under live traffic; stage it. Reversibility: introducing a facade is cheap; a full data split is near a one-way door.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Orders needs strong consistency for stock? -> Keep a synchronous reserve call with idempotency keys, or keep them in one service.
  • Do we need microservices at all? -> A modular monolith with enforced boundaries may be enough.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team with 6 "independent" services all joined the same table; each release needed a war-room until reads moved behind APIs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more tests only.
  • Hire: names the shared DB and proposes an API.
  • Strong hire: staged migration, contract tests, trade-offs and reversibility.

questions.contextHtml: Interview prompt: "Design the class model for a library: members borrow physical copies of books; a book title can have many copies; a loan has a due date and fee rules differ for students and staff; deleting a member must not delete the book catalogue; a branch has shelves with slots." You have 10 minutes at a whiteboard.
questions.promptHtml: Name the classes, draw each relationship with its type, multiplicity and reason, and say what you would NOT model.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Draws boxes with plain lines and putting Book inside Member. No lifetimes, no multiplicities.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we track individual copies? Can a copy be at several branches? Are loans history (kept after return)? Is fee logic going to change? Reservations in scope?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; state assumptions first: copies tracked, loan history kept.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (options): Book vs BookCopy split; Loan as its own entity (association class); FeePolicy as an interface.
  4. How I'd verify: Walk three scenarios: borrow, return late, delete a member.
  5. Model:
Branch <#>-- 1..* Shelf <#>-- 1..* Slot            composition (die with branch)
Book (title) 1 ---- 1..* BookCopy                  association; copy needs a title
BookCopy <>---- 0..1 Slot                          copy can be shelved elsewhere
Loan  * ----> 1 Member ;  Loan * ----> 1 BookCopy  associations (Loan is history)
Loan ..> FeePolicy                                  dependency at return time
FeePolicy <|.. StudentFee, StaffFee                realization
  1. Code (the one interesting part):

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface FeePolicy { long fee(Loan l, LocalDate returned); }
final class Loan {
    private final Member member; private final BookCopy copy; private final LocalDate due;
    Loan(Member m, BookCopy c, LocalDate due) { member = m; copy = c; this.due = due; }
    long close(LocalDate returned, FeePolicy p) { return p.fee(this, returned); }
}
fun interface FeePolicy { fun fee(l: Loan, returned: LocalDate): Long }
class Loan(val member: Member, val copy: BookCopy, val due: LocalDate) {
    fun close(returned: LocalDate, p: FeePolicy) = p.fee(this, returned)
}
  1. Prevention (design checks): Every arrow justified with ownership; add multiplicities; Loan references ids/objects but Member does not own Loans (deleting a member anonymises, keeps history).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No inheritance Student extends Member; use a MemberType with fee policy (composition). I would not put private helpers in the diagram.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Add e-books? -> BookCopy becomes an interface or digital copy type with no slot; the Loan model stays.
  • Deleting a member with open loans? -> Block, or force return; do not cascade to copies.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A library app modelled Member <#> Loan with cascade and lost 3 years of lending history on a GDPR delete request.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: boxes with unlabelled lines.
  • Hire: correct arrows, multiplicities, copy vs title split.
  • Strong hire: justifies each arrow by lifetime, avoids needless inheritance, handles deletion rules.
